Article Title: Srijan Realty launches Orizon, an 8.3-Acre landmark redefining residential living on Kolkata’s Southern EM Bypass
Article Text:
The 702-unit, 6-tower project brings 80% open space, barrier-free design & IGBC Platinum pre-certified sustainability to South Kolkata’s growing corridor.

Project at a glance

A life beyond the ordinary

As Kolkata’s residential landscape continues to evolve, emerging micro-markets are gaining prominence as homebuyers increasingly seek a combination of connectivity, convenience and well-developed social infrastructure. The Southern EM Bypass corridor, in particular, has witnessed a decade-long transformation from a peripheral suburb into one of the city’s most aspirational residential addresses, supported by expanding metro and suburban rail connectivity, dual EM Bypass access, and a maturing ecosystem of schools, hospitals and retail destinations. Against this backdrop, Srijan Realty, one of Eastern India’s most established residential developers, today announced the launch of Orizon, a 702-unit residential community spread across 8.3 acres off the Southern EM Bypass in Jagaddal, South Kolkata.Located on B.C. Roy Road in Jagaddal, with two access points off the Southern EM Bypass roughly 400 metres and 750 metres apart, Orizon comprises six high-rise towers ranging from 17 to 23 storeys, housing 702 three-bedroom residences sized between approximately 1,208 and 1,650 square feet. Roughly 80 percent of the 8.3-acre site — 85 percent including podium-level landscaping, has been kept open, an unusually low-density ratio for a development of this scale so close to the city. Shahid Khudiram Metro Station is roughly14 minutes away, with Sonarpur railway station around 15 minutes; Spencer’s, Wood Square Mall and Southwinds Galleria are all within a six-minute drive.Orizon’s design philosophy takes its name from the word “horizon,” built around the idea that space, light and an unobstructed view are increasingly scarce commodities in a city that has grown denser over the past two decades. Residences feature terrace-style and standing balconies intended to maximise natural light and cross-ventilation, while the project’s golden façade, visible from the EM Bypass — is conceived as a visual landmark along the corridor.Despite its dual EM Bypass access and proximity to South Kolkata’s commercial nodes, the development has been planned to function as a self-contained green enclave, insulated from the congestion typically associated with high-density urban corridors. Schools including BDM International and Narayana, along with healthcare providers such as Apollo Hospital’s upcoming campus, Peerless Hospital and RN Tagore Hospital, are within a 20-minute radius.At the centre of the development sits a roughly 33,000-square-foot clubhouse featuring an infinity-edge swimming pool, jacuzzi and dedicated kids’ pool, alongside a 21,000-square-foot podium-level garden anchoring a sports arena with facilities for tennis, basketball, pickleball and badminton. Indoor offerings extend to a gymnasium, yoga and meditation studio, squash court, co-working space, home theatre, library, and a dedicated senior citizens’ lounge, amenities the developer says are designed to serve every age group within a single community rather than cater narrowly to one demographic.A defining feature of Orizon is its barrier-free design, incorporating wheelchair access ramps, lift cabins wide enough to accommodate wheelchairs, Braille and voice-enabled lift controls, accessible toilets and designated accessible parking throughout common areas. Srijan Realty positions this not as a regulatory minimum but as a forward-looking response to India’s multigenerational households, where ageing parents, differently abled family members and young children increasingly share a single home and require equal, independent access to shared spaces.Orizon has been pre-certified for IGBC Platinum design, India’s highest green building rating, with features including rainwater harvesting, solar power for common areas, low-flow water fixtures, energy-efficient LED lighting, organic waste management, and EV charging infrastructure. Buildings certified to this standard typically deliver 20 to 30 percent energy savings and 30 to 50 percent water savings compared with conventional construction."Orizon reflects how we believe Kolkata wants to live today. Homebuyers are no longer choosing between space and connectivity, or between design and responsibility - they expect all of it together. Southern EM Bypass has moved past being an emerging corridor - it is now one of South Kolkata's defining growth engines, and we have been part of that story for over a decade.We have built Orizon as a community first, planned around low-density living, open space, and lifestyle infrastructure that we believe will hold its value well beyond the next market cycle, with inclusivity and sustainability designed into its foundations rather than added on at the end”, said Dinesh Agarwal, Director, Srijan Realty, reflecting on the vision behind the project.Rera number: Phase I - WBRERA/P/SOU/2026/004474 |NOTE: The information contained herein is indicative and for promotional purposes. Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Wednesday said the party stood firmly with the people of Ladakh in their demand for meaningful constitutional safeguards, including Sixth Schedule status, to protect the Union Territory’s land, employment opportunities, fragile environment, culture and identity.In a post on X, Kharge said four young people were shot dead in Leh a year ago during protests demanding democratic and constitutional rights for the people of Ladakh."A year ago, four young people were shot in Leh during the agitation for the Democratic and Constitutional rights of the people of Ladakh. On Martyrs’ Day, we pay our solemn homage to them and stand in complete solidarity with their families," Kharge said in a post on X."The judicial inquiry into the tragic events of September 24 must establish the full truth, ensure accountability and deliver justice without fear or favour. The people of Ladakh have waited long enough for their legitimate aspirations to be addressed," he added.On September 24, 2025, police in Leh opened fire during violent protests demanding statehood and constitutional safeguards for Ladakh, killing four people.Kharge said that the Congress party "stood firmly" with their demand for meaningful Constitutional safeguards, including the Sixth Schedule, to protect Ladakh's land, employment, fragile environment, culture and identity.Meanwhile, Ladakh authorities on Tuesday promised a new framework under Article 371 to provide constitutional safeguards tailored to the Union territory’s specific needs.In an interaction with prominent community members in Leh, Chief Secretary Ashish Kundra indicated broad agreement on the need for such safeguards. “The protection should cover our land, employment, culture, environment and natural resources,” he said.Kundra said the new framework being worked out “considering the aspirations of Ladakhis does not exist anywhere else in the country”.The draft is expected to be discussed at the next meeting with Ladakh groups in the first week of October. The last meeting between the Centre and Ladakh representatives was held in Delhi on September 9.

Article Title: Shouldn’t punish for refusing to sing ‘Vande Mataram’: Supreme Court
Article Text:
SC disagreed with the suggestion that the recognition of all six stanzas was not in concord with a ‘secular’ Constitution.

Courts can’t dictate what national song should be: SC

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Tuesday agreed to examine the legality of penal consequences if a person does not sing the national song due to religious beliefs or conscientious objection, but declined to adjudicate whether ‘Vande Mataram’ should comprise two or six stanzas, saying it was best left to Parliament’s wisdom.The court was hearing a petition by Carnatic vocalist T M Krishna objecting to recital of the complete version of the national song on the ground that its last four stanzas invoked Hindu goddesses which may offend the religious beliefs of some communities. The amended law stipulates punishment of up to three years in jail for disrupting or preventing rendition of the song.A bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said the field was occupied by SC’s Aug 1986 Bijoe Emmanuel vs Kerala judgment that no one could be penalised for not singing the national anthem if he showed respect to it by standing in silence.Seeking the Centre’s reply in two weeks, the bench said, “nobody’s Article 25 rights or the right of a conscientious objector should be violated”.It said the Bijoe Emmanuel case ruling had never been challenged and was still the law of the land. The Centre must consider the issue raised in the PIL from that perspective, it said.The bench added that if a conscientious objector did not sing one or all stanzas of the national song, he would not be subjected to criminal prosecution.Appearing for Krishna, senior advocate S Muralidhar argued that ‘Vande Mataram’ must be confined to two stanzas, as done by Congress Working Committee in 1937 due to strong opposition by Muslims, whose faith does not permit idol worship.The hearing was marked by the bench disagreeing with the suggestion that the recognition of all six stanzas as the national song was not in concord with a “secular” Constitution and a heated exchange between solicitor general Tu-shar Mehta and Muralidhar.Muralidhar’s argument that the law-making process, where Parliament made singing of all six stanzas of Vande Mataram mandatory, was not inclusive as it did not fully accommodate public opinion had Mehta angrily retorting that law-making could not be made subservient to the “diktat of Naxalite ideas”.Justice Bagchi was sceptical of the argument that singing all six stanzas would undermine the constitutional mandate of secularism, which is a sine qua non for constitutional governance.Justice Bagchi told Muralidhar, “Nothing can be more strong or positive secularism than the US constitution. But the American national anthem uses the word ‘God’. The national song, not national anthem, paying homage to a particular form of God will not perhaps impact secularism. But your point is about whether someone who is a conscientious objector can be subjected to penal consequences. We will examine it.”Muralidhar said all six stanzas were thrust upon people after 80 years and not singing it invited penal consequences. “That is what is most worrying,” he said.The SC said, “Penal consequences we will examine. But the state is best suited to declare what the national song is and articulate national aspirations. If these kinds of issues are debated, then this would be the most unfortunate thing for the nation. Courts cannot dictate what the national song should be.”Mehta said the petition was meant to create sensationalism and persuaded the court not to issue notice while assuring that Centre would file a response.The bench said, “We may not issue notice. But the law of the land as declared by SC (in Bijoe Emanuel case) governs the acts of the state. That declaration has not been questioned. There is no dispute as to what the national song is. It is for the democratically elected state to decide what the national song is, four stanzas or two stanzas. But nobody’s Article 25 rights or the right of a conscientious objector should be violated.It is not for the court to second-guess the national sentiment or aspirations associated with ‘Vande Mataram’.”Mehta said it was not for the petitioner to decide whether the national song should be of two or six stanzas. “Those who could not stall the amendment to Prevention of Insults to National Honours Act in Parliament are now bringing the issue to the court,” he added.
Article Summary: Sc disagreed with the suggestion that the recognition of all six stanzas was not in concord with a ‘secular’ constitution. Courts can’t dictate what national song should be: sc. Court was hearing a petition by carnatic vocalist t m krishna objecting to recital of the complete version of the national song.

Article Title: Gurugram collapses in rains while Greater Noida planned for 30-40 years: Supreme Court
Article Text:
File photo: Supreme Court

Supreme Court raises infrastructure concerns

What is the Premium FAR scheme?

Government says Premium FAR cannot regularise illegal buildings

Karnataka authorities get four weeks to respond

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday said the urban system in Gurugram collapses during rains because adequate investment was not made in infrastructure such as drainage and sewage systems. The court contrasted this with Greater Noida, saying the latter was planned with the next 30-40 years in mind.The observations came while the top court was hearing a plea challenging the Karnataka High Court's decision upholding the state's Premium Floor Area Ratio (FAR) scheme.A bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant, along with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, issued notice on the plea filed by the Citizens Action Forum.The bench, however, clarified that the additional FAR available under the scheme should not be used to regularise illegal construction.Chief Justice Surya Kant said there was no visible improvement or addition to the basic infrastructure of the township, such as roads, sewer lines and bus flyovers, despite the additional construction capacity."We have seen in Gurugram how this system collapses if any natural calamity comes.Because, without adding to this infrastructure, you are burdening the size of the plot with multiple storeys," the CJI said.He said the situation was different in Greater Noida because the city had been planned keeping the next 30-40 years in mind.The observations came amid arguments over whether Bengaluru's existing infrastructure can support additional construction allowed under the Premium FAR scheme.The Premium FAR scheme allows property owners to purchase additional construction rights beyond the ordinarily permissible FAR by paying prescribed premium charges. The stated objective is to facilitate vertical development and generate revenue for urban local bodies.FAR refers to the ratio of a building's total floor area to the size of the plot on which it stands.Senior advocate Aditya Sondhi, appearing for the Citizens Action Forum, argued that road width had effectively become the main criterion for granting Premium FAR, despite existing pressure on Bengaluru's parking, water, electricity and other infrastructure.Justice Bagchi also referred to Bengaluru's traffic problems, saying the city has a "traffic nightmare" and that this was a serious concern raised by the petitioner.Solicitor general Tushar Mehta, appearing for the state authorities, said the overall additional FAR remained capped at 0.6. He also said existing setback and parking requirements continued to apply and that developers could not simply purchase additional FAR without meeting parking and other regulatory requirements.Mehta said the money collected under the scheme would go into a dedicated fund for civic infrastructure.A key issue before the bench was whether the Premium FAR scheme could be used to regularise unauthorised construction.Sondhi questioned how the new scheme differed from the earlier Akrama-Sakrama scheme, under which unauthorised constructions were legalised. He told the court that a provision in the Greater Bengaluru Authority Act allowed Premium FAR to be used for regularising existing illegal constructions.Mehta rejected the contention and gave an assurance that unauthorised construction covered by the Akrama-Sakrama scheme would not be regularised under the Premium FAR scheme."It has nothing to do with that. Kindly record my statement. It is completely different. You can also pass directions to this effect," Mehta said.He argued that urban space was limited and vertical growth was the way forward, adding that cities were increasingly moving towards vertical development.The Supreme Court asked the Bengaluru authorities to file their response to the plea within four weeks.The case challenges the Karnataka High Court's June 15 judgment upholding the constitutional validity of the Premium FAR scheme. The high court had dismissed petitions arguing that the scheme violated property rights and reduced the value of Transferable Development Rights (TDRs).The Premium FAR scheme was introduced under Section 18-B of the Karnataka Town and Country Planning Act, 1961. The high court had held that it did not violate Articles 14, 21 or 300A of the Constitution.The NGO had argued that Premium FAR allowed developers to purchase additional building rights at rates significantly below the market cost of TDRs, thereby undermining TDRs secured by landowners as compensation for land.The high court rejected the argument, holding that a state policy resulting in fluctuations in property values would not by itself make the policy violative of Article 300A.
Article Summary: Supreme court says urban system in gurugram collapses during rains because adequate investment was not made in drainage and sewage systems. Court contrasted this with greater noida, saying the latter was planned with the next 30-40 years in mind.

Article Title: Rajya Sabha polls for 12 seats: BJP likely to retain 8 in UP, SP eyes gain, BSP at risk
Article Text:
BJP likely to retain 8 UP seats, SP eyes 2, BSP faces exit

NEW DELHI: The BJP is set to have the numbers on its side in the upcoming Rajya Sabha elections in Uttar Pradesh, with the party-led alliance expected to win eight of the 10 seats going to polls in the state. The Samajwadi Party could take the remaining two seats, based on the current strength of parties in the assembly.The Election Commission on Tuesday announced polls for 12 Rajya Sabha seats in Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand and West Bengal. Voting, if required, will be held on October 16, with the results also to be declared the same day.The BJP is also expected to add one seat to its Rajya Sabha tally by winning the lone seat from West Bengal. The seat became vacant after actor Rukmini Mallick, popularly known as Koel, resigned from the House. The Trinamool Congress had sent her to the Rajya Sabha before losing power in the assembly election held earlier this year.In Uttar Pradesh, the BJP-led alliance has around 290 MLAs, while the SP-Congress combine has about 103. A candidate needs around 37 votes to win a Rajya Sabha seat.The BJP can comfortably win seven seats, while the SP-Congress combine can secure two.The contest for the 10th seat could be closer, with the BJP-led alliance starting with around 31 votes against around 29 for the SP-Congress side.The polls could also mark the end of the BSP's representation in Parliament. Mayawati's party has no member in the Lok Sabha and its only MLA in Uttar Pradesh, Uma Shankar Singh, died in August. The term of BSP's lone Rajya Sabha member, Ramji Gautam, ends in November.Gautam is among the nine Uttar Pradesh members whose terms are ending. The others are Union minister Hardeep Singh Puri, BJP leaders Arun Singh, Geeta Shakya, Neeraj Shekhar, Brijlal, B L Verma and Seema Dwivedi, and SP leader Ram Gopal Yadav.Puri's continuation in the Union Cabinet will depend on whether the BJP nominates him for another Rajya Sabha term.The 10th Uttar Pradesh seat was held by former deputy chief minister Dinesh Sharma. It became vacant earlier this month after Sharma resigned from the Rajya Sabha following his appointment as lieutenant governor of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.The BSP had managed to retain its Rajya Sabha presence in 2020 after the BJP fielded only eight candidates for 10 seats. The move allowed the BSP and SP to each elect one member unopposed.Gautam was elected unopposed after the nomination of an SP-backed Independent candidate was rejected. The SP had then alleged an understanding between the BJP and BSP.In Uttarakhand, BJP Rajya Sabha member Naresh Bansal's term is ending. The BJP, which has a comfortable majority in the state assembly, is expected to retain the seat.The election notification will be issued on September 29. Candidates can file nominations till October 6. Polling and counting will take place on October 16, if required.
Article Summary: Bjp likely to retain 8 up seats, sp eyes 2, bsp faces exit. Election commission on tuesday announced polls for 12 rajya sabha seats. Voting, if required, will be held on october 16, with results also to be declared the same day.

Article Title: ‘We don’t condone cheating’: IIT Bombay students call for reforms after Sahil’s death
Article Text:
Back fair probe into Professor Doolla

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Oppose external political influence

NEW DELHI: Student representatives at IIT Bombay have issued an official statement following the death of student Sahil Wakode, saying they do not condone cheating or any form of academic misconduct, while calling for reforms to address systemic concerns within the institute.“We do not stand for or condone cheating or any form of academic misconduct. At the same time, the loss of our fellow student, Sahil, is a deeply tragic event that has compelled us to reflect on the systems and processes within our Institute,” the representatives said.They said the protest launched by students was not intended to justify academic misconduct, but was a collective effort to raise concerns over issues that had existed within the institute for some time and seek “meaningful and strong institutional reforms” to prevent similar circumstances in the future.The representatives also welcomed the open house held with the institute's Director and other members of the administration on Sunday, saying it gave students an opportunity to directly raise their concerns and questions.On Professor Suryanarayana Doolla, the students clarified that they had never presumed his guilt or sought to prejudge the ongoing investigation.“We stand with Professor Doolla as a member of our faculty community and believe that the investigation must be allowed to proceed fairly and impartially,” they said.The students said their demand was for Doolla to be relieved of his administrative responsibilities as Dean of Administrative Affairs while the investigation is underway. They described this as a precautionary measure intended to ensure that the probe remains independent and cannot be influenced in any manner.“The findings and appropriate action should follow from the established investigative process,” the representatives said.The student representatives said concerns arising from Sahil’s death should remain student-led and be addressed within the institute.“The loss of Sahil should not become a platform for external political interests, organisations, or narratives to shape the concerns of the IIT Bombay student community,” they said.They added that the demands had emerged from students’ experiences and concerns on campus, and that the reform process should remain rooted in the student community and the institute.
Article Summary: Student representatives at iit bombay have issued an official statement following the death of student sahil wakode. They say they do not condone cheating or any form of academic misconduct, while calling for reforms to address systemic concerns within the institute.

Article Title: National film awards will now be at tourist destinations: Ashwini Vaishnaw
Article Text:
President Droupadi Murmu presents the Best Actress in a Leading Role award to Yami Gautam for her performance in Article 370 during the 72nd National Film Awards, in Gujarat, Tuesday

NEW DELHI: On a day Ekta Nagar in Gujarat's Kevadia - where ' Statue of Unity ' holds centrestage - became the space for at the 72nd National Film Awards, information and broadcasting minister Ashwini Vaishnaw on Tuesday said govt plans to take these awards to some of the best tourism destinations across states in the future.He urged all states to send in their proposals of best tourist destinations, and prepare and execute 360 degree development plans in those areas. "The proposal of whichever state is selected, the next national film awards will be held at that tourist destination," he said.Reflecting on PM Narendra Modi's vision when G20 summit was organised in India in 2023, Vaishnaw said that at that time too programmes related to the summit were held across different states. The same is being done with the film awards and, therefore, these are being organised and will be taken to different tourist destinations in the future, he said.
Article Summary: Information and broadcasting minister ashwini vaishnaw said govt plans to take these awards to some of the best tourism destinations across states. He urged all states to send in their proposals of best tourist destinations, and prepare and execute 360 degree development plans in those areas.

Article Title: ED appeal ‘abuse of process’ in National Herald case: Gandhis
Article Text:
Rahul Gandhi, Sonia Gandhi

NEW DELHI: Congress netas Sonia Gandhi and Rahul Gandhi have said it is “abuse of the process of law” that ED has challenged in Delhi high court a trial court order refusing to take cognisance of its chargesheet against them in the National Herald-linked money laundering case.In a response filed in the high court, the Gandhis opposed ED’s revision plea saying it is “not maintainable” as trial court’s order is “perfectly legal and sound in law and does not suffer from any jurisdictional error, perversity, irregularity or illegality”.On Tuesday, Justice Sachin Datta was informed by the Gandhis’ counsel that they had filed their replies on Sept 18. HC has listed the matter for Oct 12.“Petitioner (ED) has miserably failed to demonstrate that the complaint filed by ED was maintainable under statutory provisions applicable to case. It is writ large that the words ‘private complaint’ or ‘a complaint by a public person/citizen’ do not find place in the statutory framework,” they contended.On Dec 16, 2025, trial court had held that cognisance of the agency’s complaint in the case was “impermissible in law” as it was not founded on an FIR.In its order, trial court had said ED’s probe stemmed from a private complaint, and not an FIR. Despite receiving the complaint made by BJP neta Subramanian Swamy and the consequent summoning order in 2014, CBI refrained from registering an FIR in relation to the alleged scheduled offence.ED claimed that trial court order has, in effect, given a hall pass to a category of money launderers only on ground that scheduled offence is reported by a private individual by way of a complaint to a magistrate.Opposing ED’s plea, Gandhis said this case provides the only instance where a non-statutory complaint by a private person has been made the foundation for initiating proceedings under the PMLA.
Article Summary: Congress netas sonia gandhi and rahul gandhi have said it is “abuse of the process of law’ ed has challenged in delhi high court a trial court order refusing to take cognisance of its chargesheet against them in the national herald-linked money laundering case. NEW DELHI: A heated exchange broke out between senior advocate S Muralidhar and solicitor general Tushar Mehta in the Supreme Court on Tuesday after Mehta referred to “Naxalites” during arguments in a case concerning Vande Mataram.Muralidhar, appearing for Carnatic musician T M Krishna, immediately objected to the expression and repeatedly asked Mehta to withdraw it.“Law-making is as per the Constitution. Law-making cannot be as per the Naxalites idea,” news agency PTI quoted Mehta saying. His remarks came after Muralidhar questioned the manner in which an amendment relating to the national song had been enacted.“The solicitor must withdraw the expression he just used now. This is going live. I don't want an expression of the solicitor going live. I strongly object. Let the Solicitor repeat the expression he used,” Muralidhar said.Mehta maintained that he was responding to Muralidhar’s objection to the decision-making process and said Parliament had enacted the law in accordance with the Constitution.“I do not want anyone to question...he says he is objecting to the decision-making.It is as per the Constitution,” the solicitor general said.Muralidhar continued to press for a withdrawal of the remark.“He started it. Why is the Solicitor using this kind of an expression? This does not behove a law officer. I have never heard a law officer using this expression,” Muralidhar said.“You cannot challenge the Constitution,” Mehta responded.Justice Joymalya Bagchi said the exchange was creating “unnecessary tension and emotion”, while Chief Justice Surya Kant intervened and said the bench was examining only the legal issue of constitutional interpretation.“Decorum is expected of law officers,” Muralidhar said.The bench later sought the Centre’s response to Krishna’s petition challenging penal provisions relating to Vande Mataram. It also asked the government to keep in mind a 1986 judgment that protected children from penal action if they did not sing the national anthem.Muralidhar, however, raised the “Naxalites” remark again after the order was dictated and sought to place his protest on record.“The learned solicitor used an expression which does not behove a law officer. I have to register my strong protest,” he said.Justice Bagchi replied, “We have not taken note of the comments. We restrict ourselves to the Constitutional issue.”Mehta said he was not apologetic and repeated his position.“I can repeat what I said. He said he is objecting to the way in which the decision-making was done. Decision-making was by the Parliament. I said that is the constitutional way, and not what the Naxalites want. I am not sorry about it,” the solicitor general said.Muralidhar accused Mehta of “playing to the gallery” and again protested.“Your lordships will not encourage this from a law officer,” he said.“Save your arguments for the next date,” the CJI told him.Senior advocate Sanjay Hegde, who was present in court for another matter, then intervened, saying, “To have a mind of one's own is not to be a Naxalite.”Justice Bagchi said that even if someone was labelled a Naxalite, that person would not lose their constitutional rights.Mehta clarified that he was not labelling any individual a Naxalite but was referring to an ideology.After Muralidhar left and the court moved to the next matter, Justice Bagchi returned to the issue while addressing Mehta.“I tell you, at least from my personal experience, we have continuously fought against extra-constitutional forces, both as members of the bar and of the bench. Our survival and our justification with the Constitution is to defeat these forces,” Justice Bagchi said.He stressed the importance of constitutional courts and due process, saying even people accused of terrorism were entitled to equal constitutional rights and fair trials.“Why will people come to courts and not to kangaroo courts? There are kangaroo courts. Constitutional courts have the respect and credibility. Why? Because we feel, even alleged terrorists, must have equal rights,” Justice Bagchi said.Mehta reiterated that he was referring to people who did not believe in constitutional decision-making.“Solicitor, we have not taken note of the comments,” Justice Bagchi said.“I don't know why he took it personally,” Mehta said.The bench, comprising CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, was hearing Krishna’s petition challenging penal protection given to Vande Mataram.During the hearing, Muralidhar argued that the amendment had been enacted without adequate public discussion or efforts to build a broader national consensus.“Ideally, these things should evolve as the building up of a public opinion,” he said, arguing against a “top down approach” to law-making.The court sought the Centre’s response to the plea and asked the government to consider the 1986 judgment concerning the national anthem while responding to the petition.
Article Summary: Sc hearing on vande mataram turns heated over 'naxalites' remark. Senior advocate s muralidhar and solicitor general tushar mehta in the supreme court on tuesday. Mehta referred to “nxalites’ during arguments in a case concerning vandemataram. Justice bagchi said that even if someone was labelled a naxalite, that person would not lose their constitutional rights.

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday questioned the steep markup on essential cancer medicines, with the bench describing the practice as “broad daylight dacoity” against patients. The remarks came after the court was informed that an essential cancer drug had a maximum retail price (MRP) of Rs 27,000, even though its price to retailers (PTR) was Rs 2,700, a tenfold difference.“There are essential medicines for cancer on which the MRP is printed as Rs 27,000 while the PTR is Rs 2,700. This is absolute rampage and carnage. This is broad daylight dacoity with patients,” news agency PTI quoted a bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta saying.“It is very surprising that the authorities who are supposed to take action on this are silent,” it saidThe bench said the price gap was “absolutely shocking” and questioned how such pricing could be allowed.“The MRP is 10 times the rate at which it is provided to the retailers. If this is not extortion, then what it is? People sell their houses, ornaments to get treatment,” the bench said.The observations were made while the court was hearing two petitions dealing with drug-related issues, including demands for tighter price controls.One of the petitioners also raised the issue of registered medical practitioners prescribing generic medicines, and stressed the need for greater regulation of medicine prices.Additional solicitor general K M Nataraj, appearing for the Centre in one of the cases, told the court that the government was not approaching the litigation as an adversarial matter.The bench said fixing medicine prices remained a major concern and adjourned the matter to September 29.One of the petitions seeks measures to make drug formulations more affordable by preventing alleged unethical pricing of essential medicines by pharmaceutical companies and retailers. It also seeks strict enforcement of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013, to check violations of price-control rules and disproportionate retailer margins.The other petition seeks disciplinary action against doctors for not prescribing generic medicines to patients.

Her injuries will heal, but riding a bike will not be the same again for Shivani Chauhan, who survived a road rage incident in Gurgaon last week in which a man in a car chased Shivani and knocked her off her moving bike on Golf Course Road. “I don't know when I'll start riding again, but whenever I do, I'll have that fear that this can happen again – that another car can come from behind and hit me,” she says.It’s a fear women bike riders understand, and echo, because of what they describe as “unprovoked aggression” that comes their way on roads. Riders TOI spoke to described being chased, tailgated, obstructed, challenged to race and subjected to lewd gestures simply for being women on motorcycles.Delhi-based rider Neharika Yadav said men have chased her from different angles to take photographs or start conversations, while Gurgaon rider Geetika Khurana recalled an incident of men blocking her way and revving alongside her to provoke a race. Male drivers revving their engines, driving dangerously close, honking incessantly – Mumbai-based motorcycle trainer and motivational speaker Shilpa Balakrishnan (51) describes this as a “routine” experience for woman on bikes.“Many have tried to corner me when I overtake. They behave this way simply because they see a woman riding,” she says.The India Women Rider Safety and Mobility Report 2026, based on responses from 542 women riders, found that 57% had experienced harassment on the road.For Shivani (27), who started riding only two years ago, the Sept 13 incident has forever changed the “therapeutic experience” of riding her Aprilia. “The incident keeps playing on my mind on a loop every now and then. It has affected me very badly, I think it will be a long time before I’m able to pick up the bike again,” says Shivani, who had kept her biker identity a secret on social media. As ‘Sia’, she felt freedom.Neharika, a dentist based in Delhi, and Pune-based fashion designer Maral Yazarloo-Pattrick (45) can relate. “I ride a bike because it gives me joy, not because I want to prove anything to anyone. In Delhi-NCR, we get cast into a stereotype. Even in 2026, there are men who can’t seem to digest a woman coming on two wheels. Since traffic here is dense, there are men like (Kalyan) Bainsla (who attacked Shivani) who will not give space to a woman rider. They will keep instigating you. I think they get some perverse joy out of it,” she says.Yazarloo-Pattrick says danger is a tax women bikers pay on roads and freedom is the reason they keep paying it. “Such behaviour is an everyday reality. I’m shocked that anyone in India is surprised,” she says. Earlier this month, she was returning from Ladakh when she noticed a black SUV without a number plate following her. She switched on her GoPro but did not try to outrun it. Instead, she slowed down and pulled into a petrol pump. “If someone is chasing me and I cannot safely get away, I always head towards a crowded place.”Soundari Sindy, a lawyer in her mid-30s based out of Chennai, says attitude towards women riding bikes is similar across the country. “It almost feels like we are hurting the male ego just by being on the road,” she tells TOI. A professional racer, Soundari commands a 150cc bike with her 5ft 1in frame. “Snide comments are common. There are strangers who have made fun of me, saying my feet would not touch the ground,” she says.Suparna Sarkar (39), chief instructor at a motorcycle training academy in Gurgaon, tells TOI what made Shivani’s case different was that the aggression was caught on camera. “It’s just that she had a camera, so it led to widespread anger. Girls I teach biking to often share incidents where either people tried to race from behind or they were hit,” she says. Sarkar has experienced it herself. In 2023, she was riding near Mahipalpur in Delhi when a vehicle hit her. “There were no cameras in the area. I didn’t have a camera either,” she says.Sandhya Das, a 38-year-old IT professional who rides with Soundari, agrees that the sight of her on a bike is somehow “not palatable to some men”, whether she is in traditional attire or in biker gear with a jacket and gloves. “Men have tried to zip past me and tried to throw me off balance,” she says.Chetana Naik (37) from Mumbai, who twice encountered a group of make bikers intimidating and overtaking her – in Kashmir recently and in Punjab earlier – adds, “For some men, being overtaken by a woman appears to be an insult that must be avenged. They begin intimidating us till their egos are satisfied,” she says.Professional rider Anita Krishnan says even riding gear can be misread by some motorists as an invitation to race. “They start racing with you. It could be a car or even a bike. They will whizz past you at speed, trying to entice you into a race. This is very common,” she says. For long-distance riders, she points out, jackets, helmets and boots are protection from crashes, flying debris, rain, heat and cold, not racing gear.Krishnan says she sometimes tucks her hair inside her jacket so motorists cannot immediately tell that she is a woman. “The gear also camouflages whether you are a woman. If your hair is out, only then people would know you are a woman. So, I would mostly hide my hair,” she says.For 23-year-old Anainah Batiwala, camouflage goes further. The Mumbaikar does not feel comfortable riding in shorts and, after dark, goes out in baggy clothes. “I dress like a guy in baggy pants,” she says. “I wear my actual going-out clothes underneath.”Atulya (23) remembers being scared for her life a couple of years ago while travelling from Gwalior to Hyderabad. A group of men followed her bike relentlessly for about 45 minutes on the highway. “I kept riding for about 10-15km even after I lost them. I was so scared that something would happen to me if I applied the brakes,” she says.Atulya (23) remembers being scared for her life a couple of years ago while travelling from Gwalior to Hyderabad. A group of men followed her bike relentlessly for about 45 minutes on the highway. “I kept riding for about 10-15km even after I lost them. I was so scared that something would happen to me if I applied the brakes,” she says.Atulya, who is originally from Kerala but grew up in Rajasthan, has been riding her bike all over India from the age of 18. While the incident rattled her, she decided to keep going.Delhi-based biker Meenakshi says long group rides can become particularly vulnerable on the return journey because riders who set out together often disperse while heading home. “Often, we get calls from riders asking for help from passers-by, or they call us to say that two or three people are following them,” she says. Krishnan says women travelling alone or in smaller groups also become more selective about where they stop after dark and often share their live location with family members.Organised riding groups have built formal safety systems around that vulnerability. Some assign a leader at the front, a tail rider to make sure nobody is left behind, and a marshal to keep both ends connected. “Men may have the liberty to stop anywhere, but women have to take extra precaution,” says Saify Ratlamwala, who runs riding groups in Navi Mumbai.Devika Mehta, a media professional from Noida, narrates how a BMW came dangerously close to her bike on a curved road, nearly running her off.“Remarks, lewd gestures, honking, and constant stares make our freedom rides really ugly. If they don’t hit you, they will come extremely close or follow to just mess with you,” the 40-year-old says, blaming this behaviour on “generations of patriarchal conditioning that has taught men that women must be watched, judged and corrected”. “Add weak impulse control, peer bravado, lax policing and near-zero consequences and harassment starts to feel normal, even entertaining, to them,” Devika says.Geetika (25), a PR professional based in Gurgaon, said catcalling, teasing and obstructing the way are things most women riders have gone through in NCR. “The day I took my first ride, the experience was not pleasant. A group of boys obstructed my way and challenged me to race with them by coming close and revving their bikes. Since then, I’ve only taken my bike out early morning when I’m assured of encountering the least traffic. ”Sarkar says it’s “not all bad that women just can’t ride on Delhi-NCR roads”, but agreed there is a “section of people who create nuisance” and that can happen anytime. “It’s not only a women rider problem, but a women safety and road safety issue. When people are on the road, they should behave. When someone is driving a car, there is a base, there is support, it will not lose balance. But when you are on a two-wheeler, even the minutest touch will make you fall,” adds Sarkar.Though less exposed than those on two-wheelers, women who drive cars say they have also encountered a “sense of entitlement” from strangers on the road, including cab drivers.Pooja (38), who has been driving for 12 years in Delhi, says comments are common, not because she has done anything to provoke it but because it’s a woman at the wheel. “I keep getting told by strangers that the size of my car (a Scorpio) doesn’t ‘match’ mine.”Rupali, an advertising professional from Noida, says she once deliberately slowed down to let a group of men overtake her in their car, just so she wouldn’t be harassed. This did not deter them. “They stopped and waited for me to pass, rolled down the windows and showed me their middle fingers,” the 35-year-old says. After they sped off, Rupali says, she drove at 30kmph so she wouldn’t encounter them again.Yet the hostility has not stopped more women from taking up motorcycles. Meenakshi says the number of women she sees learning to ride has increased sharply. “Three years ago, if I trained 10 women in a month, the number would be 60-70 now,” she says. The profile, according to Krishnan, is changing too, with women in their 40s, 50s and even 60s increasingly taking up long-distance riding.Dnyanadaa Mhaskar is an example of that change. The Navi Mumbai schoolteacher began riding at 41, bought a motorcycle while still on a learner’s licence and, by her own account, barely knew how to work the clutch and gears. She later borrowed her grocer’s 100cc Hero for a ride to Pune and joined an all-women motorcycling group. Now 54, she says simply: “Riding is my solace and my bike is my soulmate.”Riya Yadav, a Gurgaon-based professional biker who has been riding since she was a teenager, adds, “People need to realise that we are just riding a bike. We are not doing some rocket science. Just treat us like a normal rider.”Most of these women say they have learnt to live with the unwanted attention on roads. “I think society at large has to change for us to see any meaningful change in men’s mindset towards a female driver. Till then, women need to take utmost precautions while riding. And be brave,” Shivani says.
Article Summary: The india women rider safety and mobility report 2026, based on responses from 542 women riders, found that 57% had experienced harassment on the road. Riders toi spoke to described being chased, tailgated, obstructed, challenged to race and subjected to lewd gestures simply for being women on motorcycles.

NEW DELHI: In a crackdown on a nexus of senior officials of Punjab govt and builders relating to Greater Mohali Area Development Authority (Gmada), ED Tuesday searched multiple premises in Delhi, Ludhiana, Panchkula, Mohali and Chandigarh, including the office of Gmada and that of IAS officer and principal secretary (housing and urban development) Vikas Garg.It is probing senior officials of Punjab govt and several builders and developers in connection with alleged corruption in Gmada and for the award of projects to builders through auction, waiver of external development charges, interest charges, etc.Searches were conducted on 26 premises “related to Tirupati Infraprojects Pvt Ltd and its promoters, directors and associated persons, besides others”. The other builders under probe include Remigate Buildestates (India) Pvt Ltd, MB Infrabuild Pvt Ltd, Mera Baba Reality Associates Pvt Ltd and Mera Baba Infrastructure Pvt Ltd.“Simultaneously, searches are being conducted at the offices of Gmada and of the department of housing and urban development, Punjab, to gather evidence from the accused entities,” sources said. “Tirupati Infraprojects is also an accused in CBI and ED cases, being allegedly involved in a bank fraud to the tune of Rs 290 crore concerning a project, Radisson Blu hotel, at Paschim Vihar, New Delhi.”“Investigation has revealed that the promoters of Tirupati Infraprojects also control entities Remigate Buildestates (India), MB Infrabuild, which had acquired two prime auction sites at Mohali from Gmada and thereafter obtained substantial financial relief in respect of the dues payable to the authority,” an official said.ED has estimated suspected undue gain to the firms and the loss to the exchequer at more than Rs 100 crore. ED is also searching a consultancy firm, Tila Consultants & Contractors, which deals with various consultancy works of Gmada and is suspected to have acted as an intermediary in the scam.
Article Summary: Enforcement directorate (ed) searches multiple premises in delhi, ludhiana, panchkula, mohali and chandigarh. It is probing senior officials of punjab govt and several builders and developers in connection with alleged corruption in gmada.
